extracted.intended_audience: researchers and the academic publishing community (authors, reviewers, editors)
extracted.subtask_description: A high-level overview of the history, core steps, quality criteria, criticisms, and emerging models of scholarly peer review used in academic journals and related venues. Aimed at explaining how peer review works and what counts as quality or concern in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to journal scope and standards (editorial assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors evaluate submitted manuscripts to determine if they align with the journal’s scope and standards. Some manuscripts may be rejected at this stage if they do not meet the journal’s criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is often a first 'desk review' step where out-of-scope or low-standard submissions are filtered before peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of expert reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal editors select expert reviewers (also known as referees), often chosen for their expertise in the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer choice is intended to ensure informed assessment; editors may seek anonymity or open identities depending on the journal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess the manuscript’s overall quality as part of their evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality assessment is broad and can include clarity of writing, organization, completeness, and presentation of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess the manuscript’s methodology and whether the methods are appropriate and rigorous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers may request additional experiments or analyses to strengthen methodological validity; methodological soundness is a core determinant of reviewer recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers assess the significance of the work and its contribution to the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance influences recommendations (accept, revise, reject) and the perceived impact of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer recommendations and editorial decision outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers provide feedback and recommend one of several outcomes: acceptance, revision, or rejection. The editor-in-chief, informed by reviewer feedback and the revised manuscript, makes the final decision and may consult the editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formal recommendation categories guide the editorial decision but the editor has final authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author revisions and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: If revisions are required, authors are typically given the opportunity to address reviewers’ comments and suggestions, which may involve conducting additional experiments or analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of the authors' responses and the sufficiency of revisions influence acceptance; responsiveness is an explicit step in the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer anonymity and review model (blind vs open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional models often keep reviewers anonymous to authors; alternative models publish reviewer identities (open identities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymity choices affect bias and accountability — the page contrasts 'often anonymous' traditional review with open models used by some journals (e.g., BMJ, F1000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency / open peer review (open reports and identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review can publish peer review reports and/or reviewer identities, making the process fully or more transparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open reports are intended to increase accountability, reduce bias, and enhance transparency. Examples: Nature Communications' open reports model, BMJ's published peer review history, and F1000's open identities and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias and conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review can perpetuate bias, with reviewers potentially favoring well-established researchers or being unconsciously prejudiced against underrepresented groups; conflicts of interest among reviewers can compromise integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and managing conflicts of interest and conscious/unconscious bias is a critical quality control concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / peer review speed
rubrics_metrics.description: The peer review process can be time-consuming, leading to delays in sharing research findings; such delays are particularly problematic in rapidly evolving fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed is a trade-off with thoroughness; preprints are noted as a way to accelerate dissemination while formal peer review proceeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review primarily focuses on validity and quality but may not always ensure reproducibility of results; there are widespread concerns about a reproducibility crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites that 52% of researchers state there is a reproducibility crisis, implying the need for practices or checks that better assess reproducibility during review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints and pre-publication dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints are full-text versions posted online before formal peer review (on servers such as arXiv, bioRxiv, SocArXiv); they accelerate dissemination and are often assigned DOIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints improve speed of sharing but raise questions about the quality and credibility of unreviewed research — they represent a trade-off between rapid access and formal vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and ongoing evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publishers experiment with post-publication review, where articles are published first and then reviewed by the community, allowing ongoing evaluation and discussion after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-publication review can provide real-time feedback, help identify errors, and support continued improvement of the scholarly record (examples: PLOS, advocates like Fiona Godlee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI and machine learning to assist peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning and artificial intelligence are being explored to assist the peer review process by identifying potential issues in manuscripts, evaluating quality, and suggesting suitable reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI is positioned as an aid to reviewers/editors rather than a replacement, with potential to speed and augment checks (e.g., for methodological problems, plagiarism, or reviewer selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation tracking and impact metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation indices (e.g., Science Citation Index by ISI) track citation patterns and provide a quantitative measure of a paper’s impact, underscoring the importance of peer-reviewed articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation-based metrics are used as proxy measures of influence but are distinct from peer-review quality judgments; their presence affects how journals and researchers assess importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific norms and historical adoption (medical journals as an example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different disciplines adopted peer review practices at different times and with varying rigor; medical journals, such as The Lancet, are cited as early adopters of more rigorous editorial assessment and peer assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variation across fields in what counts as sufficient rigor, typical review practices, and speed — disciplinary norms shape review expectations.
